title: The Mokshan Regiment on the Hills of Manchuria: Waltz
author: Ilya Shatrov
annotation: The bandmaster of the 214th Mokshan Regiment led his musicians onto the parapet near Mukden as the regiment fought its way out of encirclement; seven of the 61 musicians survived. A year later he wrote a waltz in memory of his comrades. Initially received coolly, its score was then reprinted 82 times in three years. The post links to a recording with lyrics.

title: The Russo-Japanese War, 1904–1905: A Lecture by Kirill Nazarenko
author: Kirill Nazarenko
annotation: A lecture by a naval historian and St Petersburg State University professor, delivered at the Museum of Political History of Russia and published by Digital History. In 1 hour 20 minutes it moves from the causes of the war to its remembrance: Kwantung, the “Bezobrazov clique”, the night attack, Varyag and Steregushchy, the Yellow Sea battle and the surrender. Sober without being dismissive, it also supplies the idea of hindsight explored in a separate channel post.

title: MINAEV LIVE: The Russo-Japanese War
author: Sergei Minayev
annotation: An hour-long episode on the empire before the war, Port Arthur, Mukden, Tsushima, Portsmouth and the reasons for Russia’s defeat. Historians prepared the material; the presenter, trained as a historian and archivist, tells it with energy and feeling. The channel particularly recommends it for anyone wanting to understand the war in one evening, though the advertising requires patience.

title: The Russo-Japanese War, 1904–1905: Album, Commander-in-Chief’s Headquarters, 1905
author: Published by the Commander-in-Chief’s Headquarters; printed by S. M. Prokudin-Gorsky
annotation: Around 300 plates of front-line photographs, persistently attributed to Prokudin-Gorsky although he only compiled and printed the album. It offers a view from the Manchurian army’s headquarters: the Shahe and Putilov Hill with a Shimose shell bursting, trenches and shelters made of sorghum, Chinese New Year and, unexpectedly for an official publication, the retreat from Mukden to Tieling. All the plates can be browsed online.

title: Album of the Wartime Life of the XVII Army Corps during the Russo-Japanese War, 1904–1905
author: Corps of Military Topographers
annotation: A second war album associated with Prokudin-Gorsky: 54 plates and 231 photographic reproductions. His workshops made the blocks and printed it; the Corps of Military Topographers compiled and published it. It does not show his personal photographic view of the war, but does demonstrate the quality of his printing. Individual plates are available in the State Historical Museum’s online catalogue.

title: Manchuria: An Illustrated Album of the Russo-Japanese War
author: A. V. Martynov, editor and publisher
annotation: An album of 122 plates published in St Petersburg in 1906, just after Portsmouth, by R. Golike and A. Wilborg. It presents a contemporary view while the war was still raw, showing how people wanted it remembered. Digitised by the State Public Historical Library and freely available on Internet Archive without registration.

title: Nichiro Sen’eki Shashinchō (日露戦役寫眞帖): A Photographic Album of the Russo-Japanese War
annotation: A Japanese photographic album held by the National Diet Library in Tokyo. A view from the other side of the parapet: photographs illustrate the post on relieving boredom in the positions around Port Arthur, including applause from enemy trenches and “Port Arthur roulette”.

title: S. M. Prokudin-Gorsky’s Colour Photographs at the Library of Congress
author: Sergei Prokudin-Gorsky
annotation: More than 2,600 colour photographs from 1905–1915, acquired from the photographer’s sons by the US Library of Congress in 1948 and now freely available. Prokudin-Gorsky did not photograph the Russo-Japanese War, a persistent legend examined separately by the channel, but the collection offers valuable views of the period.

title: Russian Archives Electronic Reading Room: Finding Aids for RGVIA Collection 487
author: Rosarkhiv
annotation: The channel suggests beginning archival research here. The electronic reading room provides finding aids for Collection 487 of the Russian State Military Historical Archive, “The Russo-Japanese War, 1904–1905”: almost 1,500 files, from General Sakharov’s reports to Nicholas II to defender Kvatu’s memoir The Truth about Port Arthur. The same archive holds Kuropatkin’s personal papers and records of the Manchurian army’s rear services.

title: A Guide to Russian Archives on the Russo-Japanese War
annotation: A guide to what is held where: naval records in the Russian State Naval Archive, including Aurora officers’ reports on Tsushima; photographs in the Russian State Documentary Film and Photo Archive; the proposed General Commissariat in Manchuria in the State Archive of the Russian Federation; diplomacy in the Archive of Foreign Policy of the Russian Empire; and the home front in the Russian State Historical Archive of the Far East. Archives have also published document collections on Port Arthur’s defence. Much remains in descendants’ family collections.

title: Japan Center for Asian Historical Records (JACAR)
author: National Archives of Japan
annotation: A Japanese centre digitising documents from three institutions: the National Archives, the Foreign Ministry’s Diplomatic Archives and the National Institute for Defense Studies. Material includes the imperial declaration of war, Portsmouth conference records and the Nichiro Sen’eki series of operational reports, divisional journals and casualty statistics. The interface is in English and Japanese.

title: National Electronic Library (Russia)
annotation: A resource the channel’s author recommends for finding and reading pre-revolutionary books and later publications. Among its holdings is Kotwicz and Borodovsky’s 1898 booklet Liaodong and Its Ports, describing Dalian Bay a year before Dalny’s foundation.

title: A Comic Based on the Channel’s First Posts
author: The channel author’s husband
annotation: A graphic version of the opening posts, “How It All Began”, “Russia Goes East” and “Korea, Manchuria and the Timber Concessions”: from the Meiji Restoration and Sino-Japanese War to Russian concessions in Korea.

title: Video: How Fortification No. 5 Worked
author: The channel author’s husband
annotation: A reconstruction based on the channel’s post about Fortification No. 5 on Port Arthur’s western flank, one of the few land-front works completed before the war. The channel reports no separate assault, but G. S. Pilsudski’s diary records the work’s artillery service. The video shows the ditch, caponiers, casemates and parapet described in the text.

title: The Russo-Japanese War on Neolurk
annotation: The internet’s account of the war, for adults: its structure is as clear as a textbook, from the night attack to Portsmouth, but its vocabulary is very different. It reads in one sitting, makes Kuropatkin and Stessel unforgettable and gives Rozhestvensky’s justifications their own section. Entertainment rather than a source: some figures are bolder than the Japanese infantry. The channel’s advice is Neolurk for the mood, then Martin for the conscience.

title: Leo Tolstoy: Bethink Yourselves! (1904)
author: Leo Tolstoy
annotation: Written by the 75-year-old Tolstoy amid the patriotic enthusiasm of early 1904, the essay was rejected by every Russian newspaper. It failed to stop the war but outlived both war and censorship. Tolstoy writes about the enthusiasm of people who will not fight themselves and asks who wages war if every individual opposes it.

title: Misha from Nagasaki: An Article in Rodina
author: Dmitry Nikolayev
annotation: The smallest child of Port Arthur: Mikhail Mühlberg was born in the besieged fortress on 13 November 1904, baptised the day after the surrender, lived 52 days and was buried in the Russian cemetery at Goshinji Temple in Nagasaki. Using parish registers and archives, the historian reconstructed the lives of his family: a wounded father decorated with the Order of St George and a grandmother who worked in a hospital throughout the siege.

title: Port Arthur: Unexpected Findings from Literary and Archival Research
author: D. K. Nikolayev, O. V. Chistyakov
annotation: An article in the Military Historical Journal, 2010, No. 1, that failed to substantiate the legend of Port Arthur’s author: archival records showed that neither Alexander Stepanov nor his father had defended the fortress or visited the city. Another life emerged instead, that of a Guards artilleryman in the First World War, about which the writer remained silent throughout his life.

title: Konstantin Balmont: Our Tsar (1906)
author: Konstantin Balmont
annotation: Opening with “Our tsar is Mukden, our tsar is Tsushima”, the poem is still quoted as a brief verdict on the war. It cost the poet years abroad: he could return only under the 1913 amnesty marking the Romanov tercentenary. The post includes the full text.

title: “It Was Horrific”: Khodynka, 1896
author: Artyom Lokalov
annotation: A Rodina article on the crush at Khodynka Field during Nicholas II’s coronation celebrations. The channel offers it as further reading for its post on the tragedy and the Russian-Chinese treaty of 1896. Published on 30 May 2026.

title: Rodina: The Later Lives of the Imperial Family’s Executioners
author: Rodina magazine
annotation: An article dated 17 July 2018 about what happened to participants in the execution. Linked from the post on the Ipatiev House, Nicholas II and Dr Botkin.

title: Zodchiy, 1904: On Designing the Plan of the City of Dalny
author: Kazimierz Skolimowski
annotation: Skolimowski's paper appeared in issues 12–14 of 1904. S. S. Levoshko's bibliography gives pp. 141–144, 153–155 and 161–166 respectively; the original pages have not been checked here. The channel post includes plans and photographs. The link leads to a mirror of the annual volume, not the publisher's archive.

title: The Defence of Port Arthur, 1904–1905: Doctors and Nurses
author: P. V. Mandryka Central Military Clinical Hospital
annotation: Medical care in the besieged fortress: surgeon Viktor von Hübbenet’s work, shortages of staff and dressings, the hospital ship Mongolia and nurse Wilhelmina Krieg’s assistance on 203 Metre Hill.

title: Ship Logistics During the Russo-Japanese War: Rice Balls Were Served for a Post-Victory Dinner
author: Akinori Ishihara (石原明徳)
annotation: A study from Japan’s National Institute for Defense Studies, published as NIDS Commentary No. 324 on 28 May 2024. Pages 7–8 discuss supply ships, Mikasa’s menu for 30 May 1904 and cases of food poisoning. This is a modern work based on naval documents; the original medical volume has not been checked separately.

title: Finance in Colonial Dalian under Japanese Rule
author: Sun Yaoting (孙耀庭)
annotation: A bank clerk’s later memoir in the second issue of Materials on the History of Dalian. The issue’s publication date has not been established. On the checked pages, 49–53 of the library PDF, the author recalls entering banking in 1930 and describes currency circulation and access to credit. The article continues beyond this extract; the full text has not been checked. Digitised by Dalian Municipal Library.
